paragraphs: Some learning objectives combine losses by exponentiating them, averaging the results, and then taking a logarithm. This Log-Expectation-Exponential structure generalizes a familiar logarithm-of-summed-exponentials calculation to settings where enumerating all contributing items is prohibitively expensive. The paper studies how to optimize these compositional entropic risk objectives, addressing failures of existing methods involving convergence, numerical stability, and speed.

The proposed algorithm, SCENT, works with a dual reformulation expressed as a min–min optimization problem. Its central choice concerns how to update the dual variable: it uses stochastic proximal mirror descent with a Bregman divergence generated by a negative exponential function. This makes the update reflect the objective’s geometry, rather than applying an ordinary stochastic gradient step without that geometric adaptation.

For convex problems, the authors establish an O(1/√T) convergence rate and theoretically characterize advantages of the proposed dual update over standard SGD. Experiments cover extreme classification, partial AUC maximization, contrastive learning, and distributionally robust optimization, with consistent improvements over the evaluated baselines. The result connects a specific mathematical update design to effectiveness across several applications sharing this objective structure.
icml-2026-a-geometry-aware-efficient-alg.tldr: SCENT uses geometry-aware stochastic updates to optimize compositional entropic risk objectives, with a convergence guarantee for convex problems and improvements across several applications.

paragraphs: An agent’s stored experiences can become a route for manipulation. A malicious memory may look harmless by itself and influence behavior only when a particular situation arises. The resulting mistake can then be saved as another experience, giving later decisions more corrupted precedent. A-MemGuard addresses both this context-dependent activation and the feedback cycle that can make repeated attacks easier.

The framework adds two mechanisms without changing the agent’s core architecture. Consensus-based validation compares reasoning paths drawn from multiple related memories, looking for anomalies that isolated inspection could miss. A separate memory component stores lessons distilled from detected failures. Consulting those lessons before future actions gives the agent a way to correct recurring mistakes instead of repeatedly treating them as useful experience.

Across multiple benchmarks, the authors report reductions in attack success rates of more than 95%, with minimal utility cost. The contribution is a defense that uses relationships among memories and lessons from failures together. These results support the value of checking how memories influence decisions and preventing detected errors from continually reinforcing themselves.
icml-2026-a-memguard-a-proactive-defense.tldr: A-MemGuard checks related memories and stores corrective lessons to reduce memory-based attacks and interrupt self-reinforcing agent errors.

paragraphs: The paper investigates how neural networks solve dihedral multiplication, a structured mathematical task involving group operations. The authors find that both multilayer perceptrons and transformers learn versions of the same divide-and-conquer algorithm. That algorithm needs only a logarithmic number of neural representations, making the task a compact setting for examining how internal features combine into a complete computation.

Clustering neurons by their activation patterns reveals three connected levels of organization. Individual neurons respond to cosets or approximate cosets, structures that organize group elements. Collections of neurons form representations corresponding to Cayley graphs and divide the dataset into subproblems. Each representation computes an equivalence class of the answer, and the network combines these partial results linearly at its output logits.

The authors describe this as, to their knowledge, the first complete characterization of all neural representations learnable on a dataset. Its significance lies in connecting neuron behavior, representation structure, and the overall algorithm within one interpretable example. The work also advances a broader conjecture about divide-and-conquer learning for group multiplication, without claiming to prove that conjecture for every group.
icml-2026-deep-neural-networks-divide-an.tldr: The paper traces how perceptrons and transformers solve dihedral multiplication through shared divide-and-conquer representations organized as Cayley graphs.

paragraphs: Agents that use external tools need plans that are flexible enough for varied tasks and structured enough to execute reliably. Sequential execution can miss opportunities for parallel work, while unrestricted generated code is difficult to optimize and verify. Another problem appears as agents accumulate reusable skills: unverified additions can gradually damage the quality of the skill library.

EvoC2F treats tool planning as a compilation problem. The agent generates plans in a defined intermediate representation with explicit semantic annotations. That structure enables optimizations, parallel execution, and fault tolerance with soundness guarantees. The framework also turns useful code into reusable functions through a verification gate, requiring learned skills to undergo testing before entering the library.

Experiments across diverse benchmarks show improvements over existing methods and lower latency. The approach matters because execution efficiency and continued learning are handled within the same framework: plans have enough structure to support correctness-preserving changes, and experience becomes reusable capability only after verification. The reported results support this combination as a foundation for agents that improve while retaining more reliable orchestration.
icml-2026-evoc2f-compiling-tool-orchestr.tldr: EvoC2F compiles structured tool plans for efficient execution and admits newly learned skills only after verification.

paragraphs: Building a useful multi-agent system involves deciding what each agent should do and how agents should collaborate. Manual design is labor-intensive, while automated approaches can rely on rigid templates or optimize a whole workflow without accounting for differences in task difficulty. EvoMAS approaches this design problem through evolution, allowing both workflows and the roles inside them to change.

The framework adaptively selects among seven strategies: three exploration operators, three exploitation operators, and one custom operator for domain-specific transformations. Role-level evolution refines specialization and collaboration. A curriculum moves development from simpler tasks to more complex ones while maintaining stability across stages. A meta-controller called Cyber Creator formulates and reflectively updates the rules guiding this evolutionary process.

Evaluations across multiple domains report consistent improvements over existing methods while maintaining cost efficiency. The agents’ roles develop from similar actors into specialized reasoning ensembles. This finding matters because the system evolves how work is divided, alongside the workflow itself. The heuristic controller addresses the tension between an inefficient purely evolutionary search and a manually designed process that cannot readily adapt.
icml-2026-evomas-heuristics-in-the-loope.tldr: EvoMAS evolves agent workflows, specialized roles, and search strategies together, reporting stronger performance across domains with cost efficiency.

paragraphs: Multi-group mean estimation asks how to divide a limited sampling budget so that every group’s average is estimated accurately. This differs from the usual bandit objective of finding and exploiting the best option. In the setting studied here, an optimal allocation samples every group on the order of Θ(T) times. That distinction motivates algorithms that do not require a separate exploration mechanism.

The paper first sharpens results describing how accurately sample variances concentrate for subgaussian distributions, using the Hanson-Wright inequality. It also identifies a strictly subgaussian class with stronger guarantees. These results support exploration-free allocation algorithms in both non-adaptive and adaptive forms, for which the authors establish tighter regret bounds than earlier results.

The framework is then extended to contextual bandit settings, where side information can guide allocation, again with provable guarantees. The contribution is a combination of improved statistical analysis and sampling procedures suited to estimating all groups well. Experimental design and personalization are identified as potential applications, rather than presented as demonstrated deployments. The broader message is that allocation should reflect the estimation objective instead of inheriting a best-option search strategy.
icml-2026-exploration-free-algorithms-fo.tldr: The paper develops exploration-free sampling algorithms with tighter guarantees for estimating every group’s mean under a finite budget.

paragraphs: Generating a geometric diagram from text requires more than producing a plausible-looking picture. The placement of its elements must satisfy the spatial relationships expressed in the description. GeoLoom treats those relationships as explicit constraints, drawing on the use of formal languages and symbolic methods in geometry problem solving to make diagram generation more accurate and interpretable.

The framework separates language understanding from coordinate construction. An autoformalization module translates the description into GeoLingua, a formal language designed for generation. A coordinate solver then uses Monte Carlo optimization to turn those constraints into precise positions. The authors also introduce GeoNF, a dataset pairing natural-language geometric descriptions with their GeoLingua counterparts, to support this translation process.

A constraint-based evaluation metric measures structural deviation and provides mathematically grounded feedback for iterative refinement. Experiments show substantially better structural fidelity than the evaluated state-of-the-art baselines. The contribution is a connected route from a written specification to formal constraints, coordinates, and measurable geometric correctness. It makes the relationships a diagram is supposed to express central to both its construction and its evaluation.
icml-2026-geoloom-high-quality-geometric.tldr: GeoLoom translates geometric descriptions into formal constraints and solves for coordinates, improving the structural fidelity of generated diagrams.

paragraphs: Soft robotic arms can deform to operate in cluttered or confined spaces, but that flexibility complicates control. Their own bodily state can be difficult to estimate, and actuation is distributed across the arm. ManiSoft introduces a benchmark for studying how vision-language policies handle these challenges, extending manipulation research beyond the fixed morphology of rigid arms.

Its simulator combines soft-body dynamics with contact-rich interactions through an elastic force constraint. Four tasks test different aspects of deformable control, ranging from end-effector coordination to obstacle avoidance. An automated pipeline produces 6,300 diverse scenes and expert trajectories. To generate these trajectories, a high-level planner chooses waypoints and a low-level reinforcement learning policy produces the torque commands needed to follow them.

Three representative policy models perform relatively promisingly in clean scenes but decline substantially under randomization. Visual analysis links failures mainly to inaccurate visual estimates of the arm’s state and limited use of deformability when avoiding obstacles. These findings give the benchmark a concrete diagnostic role: it exposes difficulties in perceiving and exploiting a flexible body, alongside providing data and tasks for further policy development.
icml-2026-manisoft-towards-vision-langua.tldr: ManiSoft benchmarks vision-language control of soft arms and exposes weaknesses in body-state estimation and adaptive use of deformability.

paragraphs: Evaluating a policy from previously collected data becomes difficult when rewards are missing in ways that depend on their values. Observed rewards can then be a biased subset even after accounting for states and actions. This paper studies that problem in finite-horizon Markov decision processes, including target policies whose decisions can depend on whether earlier rewards were recorded.

The authors formulate a reward-dependent observation propensity model and use future states as shadow variables to identify the conditional mean reward in the full data. They also introduce a bridge function that recovers this mean without explicitly modeling the missingness mechanism. A min-max estimation procedure avoids double sampling. An estimator in the style of Fitted Q Evaluation then propagates the recovered rewards to evaluate the target policy.

The paper establishes consistency and finite-sample error bounds for the estimator. Experiments on simulated data and MIMIC-III Sepsis data show strong performance relative to existing methods. The contribution connects correction for reward-dependent missingness with sequential policy evaluation, while explicitly allowing the policy itself to respond to the history of missing observations.
icml-2026-off-policy-evaluation-for-miss.tldr: The paper develops policy evaluation methods that recover mean rewards under value-dependent missingness and accommodate policies that use missingness history.

paragraphs: Aerial image understanding has two complementary tasks: detecting objects from open-vocabulary category descriptions and locating objects referred to by richer language. In the formulations discussed here, the first provides coarse category semantics, while the second is limited to a single target. OTA-Det unifies them to support detailed textual descriptions together with detection of multiple targets.

The framework reformulates objectives and supervision so that datasets from both tasks can contribute to joint training. It also aligns language and visual content at several levels, connecting entire expressions as well as individual attributes to the image. This dense semantic alignment is intended to preserve the fine-grained meaning that category labels alone cannot capture.

OTA-Det builds on RT-DETR and adds efficient modules to extend closed-set detection into open-text detection. The authors report state-of-the-art results on six benchmarks spanning both aerial detection and remote-sensing visual grounding, alongside inference at 34 frames per second. These results support combining the two forms of supervision within one architecture while retaining the reported real-time execution speed.
icml-2026-open-text-aerial-detection-a-u.tldr: OTA-Det unifies aerial object detection and language grounding to locate multiple targets from detailed text while maintaining reported real-time inference.

paragraphs: A model can score well on broad image-description matching while still missing essential visual facts. PerceptionRubrics evaluates perception through individual, image-specific checks instead of relying on an overall semantic resemblance. It pairs 1,038 information-dense images with more than 12,000 rubrics, aiming to expose errors that can be hidden by strong aggregate benchmark performance.

The rubrics come from reference captions constructed through a Circular Peer-Review consensus process. They divide into Must-Right criteria for essential facts and Easy-Wrong criteria for fine details. Gated scoring applies sharp binary penalties when mandatory facts are missed. Consequently, getting many separate details right cannot simply average away a failure on a required visual fact.

Evaluations reveal a reliability gap: models often recognize individual elements but struggle when several requirements must all hold together. The authors also report a persistent 5% perception deficit between open-source and proprietary frontier models in their evaluation. Their gated metrics align substantially better with human judgments than conventional benchmarks, supporting stricter assessment of perceptual fidelity when judging the reliability of generated descriptions.
icml-2026-perceptionrubrics-calibrating-.tldr: PerceptionRubrics uses image-specific factual checks and gated penalties to expose perceptual failures that broad benchmark scores can conceal.

paragraphs: Composed image retrieval starts with an image and a written request to change something while preserving other relevant content. The difficulty is deciding which visual properties should change and which should remain. Existing fusion methods can lose fine details, while approaches that caption the reference image may miss implicit intent and produce repetitive result lists.

Pix2Key represents both the query and candidate images as open-vocabulary visual dictionaries. Within a shared embedding space, these representations support matching against the user’s intended constraints and reranking results for diversity. A self-supervised component called V-Dict-AE improves the dictionaries using images alone, strengthening fine-grained attribute understanding without requiring supervision specifically for composed image retrieval.

On the extended DeepFashion-MM benchmark, Pix2Key improves Recall@10 by up to 3.2 points. Adding V-Dict-AE provides a further 2.3-point gain, while improving intent consistency and maintaining high list diversity. The findings connect the quality of the image representation to both retrieval success and controllability: the method aims to honor the requested edit without collapsing the returned list into near-repetitive choices.
icml-2026-pix2key-controllable-open-voca.tldr: Pix2Key uses visual dictionaries to retrieve images that respect requested edits while preserving relevant attributes and result diversity.

paragraphs: Successful reasoning includes recovering when an intermediate decision leads nowhere. This paper studies that ability by modeling chain-of-thought reasoning as finding paths through a graph. It compares supervised fine-tuning with reinforcement learning using verifiable rewards, asking how their training signals affect the amount of computation needed to solve a problem at inference time.

In the analyzed setting, supervised fine-tuning on ideal shortest paths without negative examples fails to teach efficient backtracking. An RLVR-trained model can instead learn to recover from dead ends using only a reward for the final outcome. This yields a provable separation in inference-time computation between the methods. The distinction concerns the specified supervised training setup, rather than establishing that every form of supervised learning must fail.

The analysis also shows how RLVR can teach where difficult decisions occur along a reasoning chain, allowing better allocation of computation. Finally, reasoning traces from the reinforcement-trained model can be distilled into a base model that learns efficient backtracking too. This connects the benefit to learnable recovery behavior that can subsequently be transferred through suitable training examples.
icml-2026-provable-benefits-of-rlvr-over.tldr: A graph-based analysis shows how outcome-reward training can teach efficient backtracking that supervision on shortest successful paths alone fails to teach.

paragraphs: Training robust point-cloud recognition models requires varied examples, but mixing point coordinates directly can create physically unrealistic geometry. PSMix changes where augmentation happens. It uses a Spherical Harmonic Transform to move point-cloud information into a spectral representation, providing a different way to combine examples while maintaining their overall structural properties.

The method performs hierarchical mixing of spectral coefficients with awareness of rotation. Its design preserves global structure while varying local details, addressing the tension between geometric integrity and useful training diversity. An additional adversarial rotation optimization strategy targets challenging orientations, encouraging the recognition model to remain invariant when the same structure is presented from difficult rotations.

Experiments on ModelNet-C and ScanObjectNN-C report state-of-the-art robustness. PSMix also improves existing spatial augmentation strategies when added as a complementary component. That combination matters because the spectral method contributes useful variation alongside techniques operating directly in space. The reported findings therefore support both its standalone robustness benefits and its compatibility with existing augmentation approaches, rather than requiring those approaches to be discarded.
icml-2026-psmix-robust-point-cloud-recog.tldr: PSMix improves point-cloud robustness by mixing spectral coefficients to preserve global geometry while varying details and training against difficult rotations.

paragraphs: Determining whether an image was used to fine-tune a text-to-image model is difficult when the image was already released without protective modifications. Existing approaches may require altering the image or comparing the suspect model with its version before fine-tuning. RECOVER addresses detection without either requirement, using behavior of the suspect model itself as evidence of fine-tuning use.

The method is motivated by the finding that fine-tuning on an image teaches its denoising trajectory across noise levels. This allows the model to reconstruct that image stably even when noise perturbations are introduced. RECOVER measures robustness during inversion and reconstruction, using that behavior to determine whether the image was part of fine-tuning.

The authors report effectiveness across a wide range of experimental scenarios and consistent improvements over existing methods. The practical contribution is a non-intrusive test that does not depend on a watermark or access to an earlier model checkpoint. Its detection signal comes from reconstruction stability associated with learned image trajectories, making the suspect model’s own response central to the assessment.
icml-2026-recover-reliable-detection-of-.tldr: RECOVER detects image use in diffusion-model fine-tuning through reconstruction robustness, without modifying the image or requiring the original model.

paragraphs: Unsupervised video domain adaptation addresses transfer between video domains without supervised target-domain training. Video differences have both spatial and temporal components, so adaptation must account for how visual content and its evolution differ across domains. MetaTrans tackles these components separately while keeping the learning objective concise, using only two fundamental loss terms.

The main design work sits in the architecture. A temporal-static subtraction module separates the treatment of spatial and temporal divergence, which the authors report it effectively removes. This gives the simple objective a more specialized structure to operate on. The method’s simplicity therefore concerns its training losses, while the architecture explicitly handles the distinct sources of cross-domain variation.

Extensive evaluations, especially on cross-domain action recognition tasks, report substantial absolute adaptation improvements and stronger relative performance gains than state-of-the-art UVDA baselines. These findings support the paper’s central design choice: separating spatial and temporal differences can produce effective adaptation without an elaborate collection of loss terms. The contribution combines a compact optimization objective with a targeted architectural mechanism for video transfer.
icml-2026-return-of-frustratingly-easy-u.tldr: MetaTrans combines two loss terms with an architecture that separately handles spatial and temporal differences for improved unsupervised video adaptation.

paragraphs: A neural solver for physical fields should respond consistently when the field is rotated. Standard transformers do not enforce that relationship by construction. ReViT builds rotational equivariance into a vision transformer for grid-based PDE solving, so the model’s treatment of orientation follows an explicit symmetry design rather than depending entirely on learning it from examples.

ReViT maps scalar and vector inputs into locally invariant representations using physics-based canonical bases. This allows standard self-attention to operate without violating the intended symmetry. A hierarchical Swin-style backbone and a precomputed reference basis pyramid preserve equivariance through operations at multiple scales. The guarantees are exact for the discrete C4 group in two dimensions and chiral octahedral group O in three dimensions, with bounded approximation for continuous rotations.

Tests span two- and three-dimensional PDE benchmarks, including magnetohydrodynamics and turbulent channel flows. The authors report strong generalization and mean squared error reductions of up to 65% against the best-performing alternatives. These results connect an architectural symmetry constraint with improved predictive performance, while retaining the distinction between exact discrete and approximate continuous rotational equivariance.
icml-2026-revit-rotational-equivariant-v.tldr: ReViT builds rotational symmetry into transformer-based PDE solvers, achieving exact discrete equivariance and reported error reductions of up to 65%.

paragraphs: Data assimilation continually updates estimates of a dynamical system’s hidden state as noisy, incomplete observations arrive. SURGE considers the case where a pretrained diffusion model supplies forecasts of the system. The central problem is how to combine those generated predictions with observations so that the estimated trajectory is progressively corrected over time.

Guiding a diffusion model with an observation likelihood can favor states that fit the measurements, but it does not guarantee samples from the true posterior distribution. SURGE therefore maintains an ensemble of particles and applies Sequential Monte Carlo over complete diffusion trajectories. It computes importance weights and resamples particles to emphasize trajectories consistent with the observations, correcting the guided generation dynamics.

The paper presents this as an approximation-free particle filtering method that rigorously combines observations with diffusion simulations. At the same time, the posterior is represented by a particle ensemble, which the abstract explicitly describes as an approximation driven toward the desired posterior. The key contribution is the trajectory-level weighting and correction procedure, rather than a claim that a finite particle ensemble exactly represents every posterior.
icml-2026-surge-approximation-and-traini.tldr: SURGE uses importance weighting and resampling over diffusion trajectories to correct observation-guided forecasts toward the desired posterior.

paragraphs: Diffusion language models can decode tokens in parallel, but mixture-of-experts versions can spend considerable computation on work that does not become accepted output. At each denoising step, many experts may activate even though only a small subset of tokens is retained. TEAM targets this mismatch by seeking more accepted tokens with fewer expert activations.

Its design draws on observed consistency in expert routing across denoising steps and across token positions. TEAM combines three expert activation and decoding strategies. Together they conservatively select necessary experts for already decoded and still-masked tokens, while also exploring multiple speculative candidates aggressively. The framework is presented as a plug-and-play way to exploit these regularities in existing MoE diffusion language models.

Experiments show speedups of up to 2.2 times over vanilla MoE diffusion models, with negligible performance degradation. The finding indicates that expert activation and token acceptance can be coordinated more efficiently in the evaluated settings. TEAM’s contribution is to connect routing reuse with decoding decisions, reducing the overhead that can otherwise limit the practical value of parallel token generation.
icml-2026-team-temporalspatial-consisten.tldr: TEAM exploits routing consistency to reduce expert activation and increase accepted tokens, accelerating MoE diffusion language models by up to 2.2 times.

paragraphs: This paper examines a safety weakness arising from connections between pieces of a language model’s knowledge. A harmful objective can be supported by information spread across questions that each appear benign. The concern is that a guardrail evaluating an individual request may fail to recognize what several responses enable when considered together.

The authors introduce CKA-Agent to study this knowledge-decomposition vulnerability. At a high level, it organizes interaction as an adaptive tree of queries and uses model responses to guide exploration across multiple paths. The collected information is then combined toward the original objective. This reframes the evaluation from optimizing a single suspicious prompt to examining the cumulative effect of locally innocuous interactions.

Across the tested state-of-the-art commercial models, the authors report attack success rates consistently above 95%, including against strong guardrails. These results highlight a gap between the apparent safety of individual exchanges and the purpose served by their aggregation. The paper argues for defenses that address knowledge-decomposition attacks, since locally acceptable responses can collectively support an outcome the model would otherwise be expected to refuse.
icml-2026-the-trojan-knowledge-bypassing.tldr: The paper shows how individually benign queries can collectively bypass tested LLM guardrails, exposing a vulnerability to knowledge-decomposition attacks.

paragraphs: Hierarchical retrieval indexes help connect broad themes with detailed evidence, but building them through repeated language-model summaries can be costly and lose information. SeRAG replaces those textual summaries with a graph-derived knowledge taxonomy. Its token-free indexing approach organizes the corpus through relationships among its contents rather than generating new summary text at successive levels.

The framework first constructs a graph capturing semantic, logical, and sequential dependencies. It then minimizes structural entropy to produce an encoding tree that preserves the graph’s topology. To connect abstract communities with granular facts, it aggregates vectors using localized structural weights. This consolidates community representations without requiring generated textual descriptions of those communities.

Experiments report substantially reduced indexing overhead and stronger performance than state-of-the-art methods on complex multi-hop reasoning tasks. The result matters because the index must support both efficient organization and retrieval across connected pieces of evidence. SeRAG ties those functions to the corpus’s relational structure, with the reported gains suggesting that hierarchical retrieval need not depend on recursive language-model summarization.
icml-2026-token-free-hierarchical-indexi.tldr: SeRAG builds hierarchical retrieval indexes from graph structure and vector aggregation, reducing indexing overhead while improving reported multi-hop reasoning performance.

paragraphs: An underspecified instruction can correspond to several genuinely different user intentions, alongside many superficial ways of expressing the same solution. Topological Active Inference aims to spend clarification turns on the meaningful differences. It treats disambiguation as progressively narrowing a geometric representation of possible intents, rather than distinguishing every sampled candidate separately.

TAI applies persistent homology to sampled solutions to recover stable intent clusters while filtering short-lived syntactic variation. This recovery relies on mild separability assumptions. It generates questions that separate those clusters and chooses among them using Topological Expected Information Gain, which measures uncertainty reduction over intents. The effective search space therefore becomes K latent intents instead of N individual solutions.

Under balanced-split conditions, the framework yields logarithmic interaction complexity, O(log K). That condition matters: the bound depends on questions dividing the remaining possibilities in a balanced way. Experiments across coding, visualization, and navigation report fewer clarification turns and robustness to noisy feedback and smaller model scales. The findings support organizing clarification around substantive intent differences rather than surface diversity among possible answers.
icml-2026-topological-active-inference-f.tldr: TAI groups candidate solutions into stable intents and selects clarifying questions that reduce uncertainty over those intents.

paragraphs: Self-play SWE-RL explores how software agents can generate their own training experiences from real repositories. Its starting requirement is access to sandboxed codebases containing source code and dependencies. It does not require human-labeled issues or supplied test commands, addressing dependence on manually curated tasks and environments for reinforcement learning.

A single language-model agent learns through self-play to introduce and repair increasingly complex bugs. Instead of specifying bugs through written issue descriptions, it proposes test-suite improvements that formally define them. This links task generation to executable software behavior and provides a way to create learning experiences grounded in the repositories themselves.

The authors report self-improvement of 10.4 points on SWE-bench Verified and 7.8 points on SWE-Bench Pro, with performance above the human-data baseline throughout training. The agent also generalizes to natural-language bug descriptions absent from training. These results demonstrate progress in autonomous training-data generation and software repair. The paper presents exceeding human software capabilities as a longer-term direction enabled by this paradigm, rather than as a capability established by these benchmark gains.
icml-2026-toward-training-superintellige.tldr: Self-play SWE-RL trains an agent to create and repair repository bugs without human-labeled issues, producing gains on two software-repair benchmarks.

paragraphs: A truthful question-answering model needs to answer correctly when it knows and abstain when it does not. Optimizing accuracy alone can encourage hallucinations, while rewarding refusal too strongly can suppress answers the model could provide correctly. TruthRL treats this balance as a reinforcement learning objective, aiming to improve recognition of the model’s own knowledge boundary.

The framework is implemented with GRPO and a three-way reward that distinguishes correct answers, hallucinations, and abstentions. This gives training a signal about both successful answering and appropriate uncertainty. Reducing hallucination can therefore involve either producing the correct response or declining to answer when the required information is outside the model’s knowledge.

Across four knowledge-intensive benchmarks and multiple backbone models, the authors report consistent gains. Illustrative results reduce hallucinations from 43.5% to 19.4% and raise the reported truthfulness measure from 5.3% to 37.2%. Their analysis attributes improvement to better recognition of knowledge boundaries, avoiding the excessive conservatism observed in baselines. The finding supports treating abstention as a distinct, useful outcome within answer training.
icml-2026-truthrl-incentivizing-truthful.tldr: TruthRL rewards correct answers, hallucinations, and abstentions differently to improve truthfulness without encouraging excessive refusal.

paragraphs: An unsuccessful interaction can reflect unclear instructions, insufficient model capability, or both together. Methods that adapt only the wording or only the model parameters address one side of this coupled problem. ROSA2 treats adaptation during multi-turn interactions as joint optimization over instructions and weights, allowing clarification and parameter changes to support each other.

Its semantic stream converts noisy or ambiguous user feedback into actionable instructions. Weight updates then operate on interaction trajectories whose meaning has been clarified. The authors call this semantic pre-conditioning and prove that it strictly reduces the parameter shift required for convergence in their theoretical analysis. The mechanism links better interpretation of feedback to the amount of model adaptation needed.

Experiments across mathematical, general-reasoning, and coding benchmarks show consistent improvements over state-of-the-art baselines. Reported results include accuracy improvement of up to 37.8% and a 40% reduction in average interaction turns. These findings support coordinating language-level refinement with parameter updates: clearer feedback helps direct learning, while weight adaptation addresses limitations that changes to instructions alone may leave unresolved.
icml-2026-words-weights-streamlining-mul.tldr: ROSA2 jointly clarifies user feedback and updates model weights, improving reported accuracy while reducing the number of interaction turns.
